hero.name: Ajay
hero.who: a 24-year-old engineering graduate in Bhubaneswar who keeps planning copycat startups

story.b: Ajay and two friends from college meet every evening at a tea stall in Bhubaneswar. They want to build a startup. This month's plan is a food delivery app for the city, like the big ones but cheaper. Last month it was a quick grocery app. Before that, a ride-sharing app. Each time, they make a pitch deck and then find five other teams doing the same thing. At dinner, his uncle, who runs a printing shop, asks him a simple question: what are you making that does not exist yet? Ajay has no answer. He goes home and stares at his pitch deck, which looks exactly like everyone else's.

ask.q: Ajay keeps planning apps that already exist. What should he focus on instead?
o: Copy the most successful app but make it slightly cheaper
Look for a real problem that nobody has solved in a new way
Wait until he has more funding to compete properly
ask.why: A slightly cheaper copy fights giants on their own terms, and more funding does not make a copy original. Looking for a problem nobody has solved in a new way is where real value lies, because creating something new is worth far more than spreading what exists.

chapters.take: Copying adds more of the same. Creating adds something new.

story.h: Sunday nights at the print shop
story.b: Ajay starts spending evenings at his uncle's printing shop. Every Sunday night, tuition teachers queue up with handwritten question papers in Odia, waiting hours for them to be typed and printed for Monday tests. The typist is slow, the teachers are tired, and mistakes are common. Ajay watches and thinks. What if a teacher could photograph a handwritten Odia paper and get a clean, printable test with an answer sheet in minutes? He searches for weeks. Nothing like it exists. For the first time, Ajay is not imagining a cheaper version of something. He is imagining a thing nobody has built yet, and it excites him more than any pitch deck ever did.

ask.q: Ajay's friend wants to add food delivery too, just to be safe. What should Ajay say?
o: Agree, since a familiar idea is less risky
Do both, so they always have a backup plan
Stay focused on the new tool, since creating something new is where the value lies
ask.why: A familiar idea feels safer but adds only another copy to a crowded market, and splitting effort weakens both projects. Staying focused on the genuinely new tool gives them the best chance to create value that did not exist before.

chapters.take: The biggest value comes from making what did not exist before.

story.b: Three months in, a big startup launches a general app for typing question papers, with ads everywhere. Ajay's friends panic and want to cut their price to almost nothing. Ajay sits at the tea stall and thinks it through. A price war would leave everyone with no money. Instead, he asks what makes their tool truly different. It reads messy Odia handwriting, which the rival cannot. It prints straight to the shop's printer. It lays out tests the way local tuition teachers like, with marks in the margin. They double down on those things. The rival keeps fighting big players for English users. Ajay's team quietly becomes the only real option for Odia teachers, and they can charge a fair price.

ask.q: A rival launches a similar app with big ads. What should Ajay's team do?
o: Deepen what makes them truly different so they have no real competitor
Cut their price below the rival's to win customers
Copy the rival's features so they look just as good
ask.why: A price war drains everyone's profits, and copying the rival turns them into another lookalike. Becoming so different that the rival is not really competing for the same customers lets them earn fairly and keep building.

chapters.take: Do not fight rivals on price. Be so different there is no fight.

story.b: An investor tells Ajay to launch across all of India at once. Ajay thinks about it and does the opposite. He picks one neighbourhood, Saheed Nagar, which has about forty tuition centres within a few kilometres. His goal is simple: make every one of them love the tool. He visits each centre himself, trains the teachers on Sunday afternoons and fixes their complaints within a day. Within two months, thirty-two centres use it every week, and teachers start recommending it to friends in Cuttack. Only then does Ajay plan a second neighbourhood. Being the favourite in one small area feels far stronger than being a tiny name nobody knows across the whole country.

ask.q: A friend building a hostel laundry app wants to launch in twenty cities at once. What should Ajay suggest?
o: Launch everywhere quickly before someone copies the idea
Win one college campus completely, then expand step by step
Wait until the app is perfect for every possible city
ask.why: Launching everywhere spreads a small team thin, so nobody truly loves the product. Waiting for perfection delays learning. Winning one campus completely brings loyal users and real lessons, and from that strong base they can grow outward.

chapters.take: Dominate a small market first, then grow outward.

story.b: Everyone tells Ajay the same thing: tuition teachers in small towns will never pay for software. They only use free apps. Even his uncle agrees. But Ajay has spent months watching teachers pay the typist two hundred rupees a paper and wait three hours for it. He believes something most people reject: teachers will happily pay if a tool gives them their Sunday nights back. He decides to test it rather than argue. He offers a monthly plan to twenty teachers. Seventeen pay. One tells him she now has dinner with her children on Sundays. Ajay realises his biggest advantage is a truth most people around him do not yet see.

ask.q: Ajay holds a belief that most people around him reject. What should he do with it?
o: Test it with real customers in a small, practical way
Drop it, since so many people disagree
Assume he is right and spend all his money building on it
ask.why: Dropping an idea just because others disagree may throw away the very insight that makes it valuable, and betting everything without checking is reckless. Testing it with real customers shows whether he has found a hidden truth worth building on.

chapters.take: The best ideas often hide in truths most people do not see yet.

story.b: The tool is good, but growth has stalled. Ajay's team wants to keep adding features and hope word spreads. Ajay sits down and writes a definite plan for the next twelve months: which towns, in what order, and exactly how teachers will hear about the tool. The answer is already in front of him. Every printing and photocopy shop near a tuition centre meets teachers every week. He offers those shop owners a small share of each subscription for setting teachers up. Within weeks, shopkeepers in Cuttack and Puri are showing teachers the app on the spot. A great tool, Ajay learns, still needs a smart road to its customers.

ask.q: Ajay's teammate says a great product sells itself. What is the better approach?
o: Keep adding features until customers arrive on their own
Spend everything on big advertisements across the state
Make a clear plan and use a channel that already reaches teachers
ask.why: Extra features do not help if customers never hear of the product, and big ads can burn money without reaching the right people. A clear plan plus a channel teachers already use, like the print shops, turns a good product into a growing one.

chapters.take: A great product still needs a clear plan and a smart way to reach people.

story.b: Weeks later, Ajay is back at his uncle's printing shop on a Sunday night. There is no queue. Teachers send photos of their handwritten papers from home and pick up printed tests ten minutes later. His uncle, who once asked what Ajay was making that did not exist, now earns a share of every subscription and tells every customer about it. Seventy tuition centres across three towns use the tool. At the tea stall, Ajay's friends no longer talk about delivery apps. Instead, they argue about which Odia town comes next, and whether the tool could one day read Bengali or Telugu handwriting. They are building something that was not there before.

chapters.take: Original ideas, started small and sold smartly, can change real lives.
